items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the function [MATH: y=f(x)] whose graph is shown below. How can we plot the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/54b34afb66b90c1c47a9fade7c956a7b]

Content:
We can use some points on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] to find the corresponding points on the graphs of [MATH: y=f(2x).]

Content:
For example, let's take the point [MATH: (-2,0).] The fact that it lies on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] means [MATH: f(-2)=0.] Then, if [MATH: x={\color{red}-1},] we have
[MATH: f(2x) = f(2\cdot({\color{red}-1})) = f(-2) = 0.]

Content:
This means the point [MATH: ({\color{red}-2},0)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: ({\color{red}-1},0)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(2x).]

Content:
So, for each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] there will be a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)] with the same [MATH: y]-value and one half the [MATH: x]-value:

Content:
[MATH: Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]|Points on [math]y=f({\color{red}2}x)[/math]; (− 2, 0)|(− 1, 0); (0, 2)|(0, 2); (1, 2)|(0.5, 2); (4, − 3)|(2, − 3)]

Content:
Finally, we can plot the points and draw the graph of [MATH: y = f(2x){:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/93bd9f97cc2b5bd149b961e7c0d7ad47]

Content:
The graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)] is the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] horizontally scaled by a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
Equivalently, we can say that the original graph is compressed by a scale factor of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
In general, the transformation [MATH: y=f(kx)] scales the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] horizontally by a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{k}.]

Content:
- If [MATH: k] is greater than [MATH: 1,] the graph is compressed (or squished) towards the [MATH: y]-axis by a scale factor of [MATH: k.]
- If [MATH: k] is between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the graph is stretched away from the [MATH: y]-axis by a scale factor of [MATH: k.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

The function [MATH: y = f\left(\dfrac{1}{4}x\right)] represents a stretch of the function [MATH: y = f(x)] by a factor of [MATH: 4] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis. This has the effect of multiplying the [MATH: x]-coordinates of all points on [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: 4.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: y=f(x)] whose graph is shown below. How can we plot the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/54b34afb66b90c1c47a9fade7c956a7b]

Content:
We can use some points on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] to find the corresponding points on the graphs of [MATH: y=f(2x).]

Content:
For example, let's take the point [MATH: (-2,0).] The fact that it lies on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] means [MATH: f(-2)=0.] Then, if [MATH: x={\color{red}-1},] we have
[MATH: f(2x) = f(2\cdot({\color{red}-1})) = f(-2) = 0.]

Content:
This means the point [MATH: ({\color{red}-2},0)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: ({\color{red}-1},0)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(2x).]

Content:
So, for each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] there will be a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)] with the same [MATH: y]-value and one half the [MATH: x]-value:

Content:
[MATH: Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]|Points on [math]y=f({\color{red}2}x)[/math]; (− 2, 0)|(− 1, 0); (0, 2)|(0, 2); (1, 2)|(0.5, 2); (4, − 3)|(2, − 3)]

Content:
Finally, we can plot the points and draw the graph of [MATH: y = f(2x){:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/93bd9f97cc2b5bd149b961e7c0d7ad47]

Content:
The graph of [MATH: y=f(2x)] is the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] horizontally scaled by a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
Equivalently, we can say that the original graph is compressed by a scale factor of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
In general, the transformation [MATH: y=f(kx)] scales the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] horizontally by a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{k}.]

Content:
- If [MATH: k] is greater than [MATH: 1,] the graph is compressed (or squished) towards the [MATH: y]-axis by a scale factor of [MATH: k.]
- If [MATH: k] is between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the graph is stretched away from the [MATH: y]-axis by a scale factor of [MATH: k.]

---
